analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prices for expensive brand-name drugs and adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 230-192 in December 2019, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the government negotiate maximum prices for 25 to 50 of the costliest brand-name drugs with no generic competition and for insulin, capping those prices at about what other wealthy countries pay. It would have penalized drug companies that raise prices faster than inflation, capped seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs, and added dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare. It passed the House in December 2019 but never received a vote in the Senate, and died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would benefit most: the government would negotiate maximum prices for 25 to 50 of the costliest brand-name drugs with no generic competition and for insulin, capping those prices at roughly what other wealthy countries pay [S3]. Beneficiaries would get a lower out-of-pocket cap with no cost-sharing above it, expanded premium and cost-sharing subsidies for low-income enrollees, and new Medicare coverage for dental, vision, and hearing care [S3]. People with private insurance could also get the negotiated prices on selected drugs unless their insurer opted out [S3]. Low-income and rural communities would gain from community health center funding, an opioid response fund, and school mental health grants [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and people on private insurance

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires HHS to negotiate maximum prices for insulin and for at least 25 of the costliest single-source brand-name drugs starting in 2023, rising to at least 50 in 2024, capping each drug's price at no more than 120% of the average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the UK, or 85% of the U.S. average manufacturer price where international data is unavailable.

Manufacturers that refuse to negotiate face an excise tax on their drug sales that escalates from 65% to 95% of the sale price, on top of civil monetary penalties, making noncompliance commercially untenable.
Drug companies must pay Medicare rebates for drugs costing $100 or more whose prices rise faster than inflation, and must report price increases at least 30 days before they take effect.
Medicare beneficiaries get a lower annual out-of-pocket threshold with no cost-sharing above it under the drug benefit, plus installment-payment options for coinsurance.
Medicare coverage expands to dental and oral health services, hearing aids and hearing treatment, and eyeglasses and vision services.
The bill expands premium and cost-sharing subsidies for low-income Medicare beneficiaries and automatically qualifies certain residents of U.S. territories.

The bill funds NIH and FDA innovation programs through the end of the decade, creates an Opioid Epidemic Response Fund, adds community health center funding through 2025, and funds school mental health and trauma services.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost: companies that refused to negotiate would face an excise tax on their sales that escalates from 65% to 95% of the price, plus civil penalties [S4]; manufacturers of drugs whose prices rise faster than inflation would owe Medicare rebates [S3]; and all makers of high-cost Medicare drugs would face new price and spending reporting requirements [S3]. Pharmacy benefit managers would lose the ability to profit from spread pricing in Medicaid [S3]. Some of the cost would ultimately come back to consumers in the form of lower federal funding for NIH, FDA, and opioid programs being tied to the new drug savings [S3].

drawbacks.text: The industry's core objection, raised in a floor motion by Rep. Fred Upton, was that government-set price caps could reduce development of new drugs; the motion sought to delay implementation until the HHS Secretary certified the program would not result in fewer new drug applications for unmet medical needs, and it failed 196-226.

The price negotiation program is narrow: it covers at most 25 to 50 selected single-source brand-name drugs a year plus insulin, and private insurers may opt out of offering the negotiated prices, so most prescription drug spending is untouched.

The bill bars judicial review of the selection of drugs, the determination of negotiation-eligibility, and the determination of maximum fair prices, leaving HHS pricing decisions outside court challenge.

A price cap pegged to foreign prices means U.S. prices fall to levels partly set by other governments' negotiation systems, which the industry argues shifts more R&D burden onto American consumers rather than lowering it globally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers and Medicare are concrete and large: government-negotiated prices anchored to international benchmarks on the costliest drugs, inflation rebates, a hard out-of-pocket cap, and brand-new dental, vision, and hearing benefits. The honest cost is the risk that lower expected returns slow the development of future drugs, especially since the bill relies on foreign price data from six countries; the bill's defenders pointed to its NIH and FDA innovation funding, but that money is capped while the price cuts are open-ended. The design is narrow in scope, covering only selected drugs and letting private plans opt out. The bill's most serious weakness, though, was never tested: it died in the Senate without a vote or a hearing on these tradeoffs, so the American public got none of the benefits and absorbed none of the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 230-192, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House passed H.R. 3 on December 12, 2019, 230 to 192, with 228 of 235 House Democrats voting yes and only 2 of 197 voting Republicans joining them.
The Senate received the bill on December 16, 2019, and it was not read a second time and placed on the calendar until September 8, 2020.
No further Senate action followed; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
A Republican motion to recommit the bill to committee to delay implementation pending a certification about new drug applications failed 196-226 just before passage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept the status quo in which Medicare is barred from negotiating drug prices and no inflation rebates, out-of-pocket cap, or new Medicare benefits took effect. The 191 House Republicans who voted no were spared a recorded vote in the Senate, which never happened.

industries.note: The bill imposed the industry's core losses: government-negotiated maximum prices set near international levels, an excise tax reaching 95% of sales for companies that refuse to negotiate, inflation rebates to Medicare, and price transparency reporting. The industry campaigned against the bill and it died before a Senate vote.
The bill required pass-through pricing and banned spread pricing in Medicaid, the practice of billing the program more than the pharmacy was paid. That revenue disappears under the bill.

Insurers covering selected drugs would have to apply the negotiated maximum fair price to cost-sharing, but any group or individual plan could affirmatively opt out of the program drug by drug, so the bill leaves their role intact while lowering some of their drug costs.

The bill temporarily increased Medicare Part B payment for certain biosimilars, and a selected drug stops being subject to negotiated pricing once two generics or biosimilars reach the market, encouraging generic and biosimilar entry.
The bill provided specified funds for the Community Health Centers Fund through fiscal 2025, which serves low-income and uninsured patients.
